findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is and gives a few reasons to care. This is the page's strongest part for that reader.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Both the title and the main heading are about firstmate, a project the newcomer probably hasn't heard of. Someone visiting Athena's own site would expect to see Athena described first, so the heading could make them think they've landed on the wrong page.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the H1 of the same text

findings.text: The page does say why it exists: it is a demonstration of what Athena can do. But that leaves most of the page as evidence about Athena, not an explanation of it. The rest of what Athena does (taking requests, a second model checking the work, cost records) gets only one sentence.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Almost all of the page is a detailed state-machine study of firstmate's internals: exit codes, lock behaviour and the pending-close replay. A newcomer to Athena has to scroll past all of it to reach the Next steps section. The "Next step" link in the header softens this, but only partly.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (cards t1–t11), "Why it is built this way" and "Claims and sources" (c1–c44)

findings.text: Near the top there is a link that jumps to the next steps, and that section gives a concrete route: the repo link, `./setup.sh` and `athena ask "add a changelog"`. So the newcomer can find out what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader has already cloned the repo. It gives no clone command and no requirements, such as a Rust toolchain or the AI model access or keys that the opening paragraph implies. A newcomer can't be sure the steps will work as written.
findings.source: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: The firstmate summary is well built for strangers: it defines terms before they are used, follows one piece of work from start to finish, and lists what fails and what has no limit. It is easy to read even though it is not what an Athena newcomer came for.
findings.source: Heading "Start here" and the "Words used first" list

findings.text: The page openly says what it does not know, here and in "Limits of this study" ("every claim is marked read", nothing run). This makes the traceability claim believable and shows Athena's approach well.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: Some guidance sentences use the study's own terms, such as "the model" and "deciders", without explaining them. A first-time reader will have to read these sentences twice.
findings.source: "The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading." and "Done and Reopened both carry the tag "ends the task": the model shows no move out of either."
